drills.q: A production service's event loop appears to freeze periodically -- no tasks make progress for a stretch, then all resume at once. Diagnose.
drills.a: A synchronous blocking call (non-async DB driver, time.sleep(), a CPU-bound loop) ran inside a coroutine with no await, monopolizing the single event-loop thread. Fix: use a genuinely async-native library, or offload via asyncio.to_thread()/run_in_executor() so the loop's thread stays free.

drills.q: A background task that was explicitly cancelled keeps running invisibly and its cleanup never seems to happen. What's the likely bug?
drills.a: The task's except CancelledError block didn't re-raise (or a broader except Exception swallowed it), so the task reports as completed normally instead of cancelled. Fix: always re-raise CancelledError after any cleanup logic.

drills.q: Process memory grows steadily during a downstream dependency's slowdown and only recovers once it speeds back up. What's the asyncio-specific cause and fix?
drills.a: An unbounded asyncio.Queue or unthrottled task-creation loop keeps enqueuing/spawning work faster than the slowed consumer can drain it, so memory grows in proportion to accumulated backlog. Fix: bounded asyncio.Queue(maxsize=N) so put() itself suspends the producer once full, and/or a semaphore capping concurrent in-flight work.

drills.q: Concurrent requests to a third-party API intermittently get HTTP 429 even though the service stays under its configured concurrency limit. Diagnose.
drills.a: A semaphore caps concurrency (in-flight count) but not rate (requests started per second) -- fast-completing requests under a low concurrency cap can still exceed a per-second rate limit. Fix: add token-bucket rate limiting targeting requests-per-second, layered alongside the concurrency semaphore, not instead of it.

drills.q: You're building an LLM proxy that fans out one request to three providers concurrently, returning the first success and cancelling the losers. What could go wrong with a naive implementation?
drills.a: Simply returning on first success without explicitly cancelling and awaiting the other two tasks leaves them running as orphaned background work (open connections, consumed rate-limit budget). Each provider call's own cancellation handling must also re-raise CancelledError after cleanup for cancellation to actually terminate the underlying request rather than leaving it running server-side.

drills.q: In the fan-out-and-cancel-losers pattern, what happens if a 'losing' provider call had already triggered a billable side effect before being cancelled?
drills.a: Cancellation only stops the client-side coroutine's further execution -- it does not undo a side effect that already occurred server-side before cancellation was delivered. The design needs explicit accounting (logging which providers were invoked regardless of outcome) or a compensating cleanup call, not an assumption that client-side cancellation erases losing-branch side effects.

drills.q: A bounded asyncio.Queue is already in place but memory still grows under a downstream slowdown. What else could be the cause?
drills.a: Check for a separate unbounded resource accumulating independently of the queue -- e.g. unbounded concurrently-created tasks each holding per-task memory (large payloads, open connections) while genuinely waiting on the bounded queue's put(), or an uncapped connection pool opening new connections to compensate for slow ones. A bounded queue addresses one backpressure point, not every unbounded-growth path.

drills.q: Why can cleanup code inside an except CancelledError block itself be interrupted, and what's the mitigation?
drills.a: Any await inside the cleanup block is itself a new suspension point where a second cancellation could interrupt cleanup before it finishes (e.g., a cleanup awaiting a lock release could get cancelled again before that release completes, leaving the lock held). Mitigation: asyncio.shield() around the critical cleanup operation, or restructure cleanup to use synchronous, fast resource-release calls instead of awaitable ones where possible -- applied carefully, since shielding the wrong scope can itself prevent cancellation from ever completing.
